passages.text: Contouring quality assurance methodology based on multiple geometric features against deep learning auto-segmentation
Background:

Contouring error is one of the top failure modes in radiation treatment. Multiple efforts have been made to develop tools to automatically detect segmentation errors. Deep learning-based auto-segmentation (DLAS) has been used as a baseline for flagging manual segmentation errors, but those efforts are limited to using only one or two contour comparison metrics
Purpose:
The purpose of this research is to develop an improved contouring quality assurance system to identify and flag manual contouring errors.
Methods and Materials:

DLAS contours were used as a reference to compare with manually segmented contours. A total of 27 geometric agreement metrics were determined from the comparisons between the two segmentation approaches. Feature selection was performed to optimize the training of a machine learning classification model to identify potential contouring errors. A public dataset with 339 cases was used to train and test the classifier. Four independent classifiers were trained using 5-fold cross validation, and the predictions from each classifier were ensembled using soft voting. The trained model was validated on a held-out testing dataset. An additional independent clinical dataset with 60 cases was used to test the generalizability of the model. Model predictions were reviewed by an expert to confirm or reject the findings.
Results:

The proposed machine learning multiple features (ML-MF) approach outperformed traditional non-machine-learning-based approaches that are based on only one or two geometric agreement metrics. The machine learning model achieved recall (precision) values of 0.842 (0.899), 0.762 (0.762), 0.727 (0.842), and 0.773 (0.773) for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible contours, respectively compared to 0.526 (0.909), 0.619 (0.765), 0.682 (0.882), 0.773 (0.568) for an approach based solely on Dice similarity coefficient values. In the external validation dataset, 66.7%, 93,3%, 94.1%, and 58.8% of flagged cases were confirmed to have contouring errors by an expert for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible contours, respectively.
Conclusions:

The proposed ML-MF approach, which includes multiple geometric agreement metrics to flag manual contouring errors, demonstrated superior performance in comparison to traditional methods. This method is easy to implement in clinical practice and can help to reduce the significant time and labor costs associated with manual segmentation and review.
INTRODUCTION

Accurate organ-at-risk (OAR) segmentation is a vital step in radiation therapy treatment planning. While higher radiation doses lead to improved local tumor control, the increase in normal tissue toxicity may lead to higher morbidity and reduce overall survival. With the advancement of radiation therapy techniques, such as intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) and stereotactic body radiation therapy, higher doses can be achieved while sparing nearby OARs; however, the resulting sharper dose gradients can have an impact on tumor control probabilities and normal tissue complication probabilities when structures are contoured incorrectly. In current clinical practice, the main method of segmenting OARs is through manual contouring, which is a tedious and time-consuming process. Contouring errors result from multiple factors, including fatigue and lack of training. A recent report from the American Association of Physicists in Medicine task group TG-275 listed “Wrong” contouring as one of the top failure modes that require attention during the initial plan/chart review. Although the OAR contours created by dosimetrists or residents are usually reviewed by attending physicians, the time-consuming nature of a thorough slice-by-slice review may result in missed segmentation errors. This effect can be compounded in therapy techniques like online adaptive therapy, where the planning process is rushed to minimize changes in anatomy while the patient is on the table. Therefore, it is necessary to establish an automated and effective quality assurance (QA) method for OAR segmentation during treatment planning.

Multiple efforts have been made to develop tools to automatically detect segmentation errors, including determining the tolerance ranges of image and shape features from populations and flag outliers, generating sets of statistical decision criteria based on shape metrics for each OAR.,, and training group-wise conditional- and image texture feature-based random forest classifier models. Recently, Nourzadeh et al established a knowledge-based quality control system comprised of group-wise inference and anomaly detection modules, based on shape, image, and relational features. A common challenge for each approach is the existence of large variabilities in features, such as size, shape, and relative location among populations. Further, large variations in said features can exist within the same patient. As a result, the acceptable range for many metrics can be too large for practical error detection. Conversely, many contours deemed clinically unacceptable may still have reasonable shapes and locations relative to other organs, and metrics for these cases may lie within the acceptable range. Therefore, these approaches, while effective in capturing gross contouring errors, usually exhibit a poor overall accuracy.

Recently, deep learning-based auto-segmentation (DLAS) methods have demonstrated success in generating contours that are similar to, or better than, those generated by human experts. Further, DLAS methods have been explored as a baseline for flagging manual segmentation errors. For example, Rhee et al computed Dice similarity coefficients (DSC) between DLAS- and clinically validated multiatlas-based auto-contouring system (MACS)-generated contours, and found that the accuracy of the clinically validated MACS contours was strongly associated with the DSC values using DLAS as reference. The average area under curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity values achieved were 0.98, 0.81, and 0.99, respectively for detecting clinically unacceptable contours requiring major editing; however, these values drop to 0.85, 0.80, and 0.61, respectively for detecting contours that require only minor editing.

Studies have shown that a single geometric index, such as DSC or Hausdorff distance (HD), is not predictive of clinically meaningful endpoints, or physician-reported assessments. For example, it has been shown that DSC values do not fully capture the discrepancy between contours. A study by Thor et al showed that there can be significant differences in the clinical acceptability in heart contours sharing similar DSC scores. A separate study by Men et al used both DSC and HD values as the metrics to flag thoracic segmentation outliers. Here, they determined the mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) of DSC and HD values in their validation data set and determined contour passing criteria of DSCtest > μDSC − 1.96σDSC and HDtest < μHD + 1.96σHD. This joint-metric approach achieved AUC, sensitivity, and specificity values of 0.95–0.97, 0.95–1.00, and 0.92–0.98 for thoracic OARs, respectively; however, it is not clear if the success of this approach is achieved due to the anatomic sites studied or the inclusion of the HD values. This suggests that a comprehensive evaluation of contour agreement metrics may be the key to fully examining the clinical readiness of contours. Multiple studies have demonstrated the success of the machine learning (ML) approach, from mining multiple quantitative and heterogeneous metrics for better outcome prediction to predicting IMRT QA passing rates. However, to our knowledge, no such study has been performed on mining contour comparison metrics with DLAS contours to identify contouring errors.

In this study, we propose a ML-based approach to achieve a more accurate flagging of manual contour errors by evaluating multiple geometric indices between manual and DLAS contours, referred to as a ML-multiple features (ML-MF) model. Clinical contours from a public dataset on the cancer imaging archive (TCIA) were used to train and test our segmentation QA tool. Given the challenges associated with segmentation in the head and neck (HN) region, we used OAR structures from this region to test the full capabilities of our approach. The performance achieved by the ML-MF approach was evaluated using recall, precision, and accuracy, and then was compared against similar approaches from the literature. Further, the error flagging capability of our segmentation QA tool was tested on clinical contours in our clinical practice.
METHOD AND MATERIALS
This study has received Institutional Review Board approval (IRB#: 43009).
Deep learning auto-segmentation model

In this study, we used the commercial DLAS software INTContour (Carina Medical LLC, Lexington, Kentucky) to create OAR contours for comparing and flagging of manual contouring errors. INTContour’s DLAS models are built using convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which use a 3D UNet model architecture that has five encoding and five decoding blocks. It has exhibited excellent contouring accuracy on multiple anatomical sites. Specifically, for HN structures, INTContour’s DLAS model was validated on multiple public and private datasets. The DSC and HD95 values achieved by INTContour for structures used for this study are listed in Table 1. The mean and standard deviation of the DSC values and HD95 values were used in contour QA method by Men et al to flag contour errors as a comparison.
Imaging data

A public HN dataset (HN-PET-CT) from TCIA was used for this study. This collection comprises 339 computed tomography (CT) images from four institutions. Considering the common side effects experienced by HN patients, the brainstem, parotids, and mandible were selected as key critical structures to examine in this study. As part of the central nervous system, brainstem contour quality is one of the major concerns for HN patients. Parotids, as serous salivary glands, are very sensitive to radiation, and radiation treatment often leads to xerostomia and affects the quality of patient life. Osteoradionecrosis of the mandible is considered a serious complication of radiation therapy in HN patients.

Contouring other structures

The existing brainstem, parotids (left and right), and mandible contours were reviewed and judged based on institutional contouring guidelines. The clinical acceptability of each contour was evaluated based on the criteria defined by the invited radiation oncologist as well as considering HN contouring inter-observer variation. Contours are considered “unacceptable” if they meet one or more of the following:

The differences in criteria for lateral contouring distance between brainstem, mandible and parotids are due to increased inter-observer variation for the parotids. The lateral over/under contouring distance is defined as the maximum of the minimum surface distance at any point in the test contour compared against the invited physician’s hypothetical reference contour.
Machine learning based multiple features contour QA model

In this study, we randomly selected 80% of the CT images to train the ML-MF model using stratified sampling to preserve the class ratios from unbalanced classes. The training data were then split as a stratified k-fold (k=5) cross-validation dataset for training and validation. The performance of the trained model was evaluated using a testing dataset comprising the remaining 20% of the CT images.

A flowchart of the proposed ML-MF QA model is illustrated in Figure 1. Comparison metrics were computed from TCIA manual and DLAS segmentations, while the contour acceptability labels were generated from human evaluation. To reduce the computational cost of training, and improve the performance of the model, feature selection was performed on the geometric agreement metrics (as described in Sec. D). Aside from model parameters initialized and updated during the process of model training, model hyperparameters also directly determine the performance and training process of machine learning classification models. There are four different groups of hyperparameter sets corresponding to each of the four classification models, support vector machine (SVM), random forest classifier (RFC), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), and multi-layer perception (MLP). To determine the ideal set of hyperparameters for each model, we performed exhaustive grid (SVM, KNN, MLP) and randomized search (RFC) analyses to generate candidate hyperparameter sets. We then tested the classification performance of each model using 5-fold stratified cross-validation. The hyperparameter set with the highest mean AUC in the cross-validation dataset was selected. Once the hyperparameters were determined, those models were trained using the full training dataset with the selected hyperparameter sets. The predictions of the four trained classifiers were then ensembled using a soft voting scheme:  where wj is the weight assigned to the jth classifier, and pij is the predicted probability for the jth classifier for the ith class labels (i ∈ {0,1}). Uniform weights were assigned to each classifier. The prediction thresholds were derived and averaged from each k-fold ROC curve in the cross-validation dataset using the point nearest to (0,1) on the ROC curve. The machine learning classifiers were built in Python using the Scikit-learn module.
Feature selection

Comparisons between DLAS and manually segmented contours were performed using an in-house MATLAB tool (MathWorks, Natick, MA). From these comparisons, a total of 27 geometric agreement metrics were generated. These metrics include volumetric DSC, precision, recall, 90%−100% undirected Hausdorff distance (HDx), mean surface distance (MSD), and Surface DSC (SDSCτ) with a varying tolerance τ from 0.5–6 mm using a 5mm step. Some features, such as the HDx, are highly colinear and correlated features. It has been reported that the linear dependence between features leads to instability and redundancy in models. It is reasonable to assume the machine model can obtain the same information from a correlated feature. Therefore, feature selection was performed to reduce the computational resources required to train a model and the likelihood of overfitting resulting from highly correlated features.

Hierarchical clustering using Spearman rank-order correlations was performed to select key features from collinear clusters. The distance metrics are computed using   where the values of dab range from 0 to 1. A dab of 0 indicates perfectly a collinear relationship, while a value of 1 indicates a non-collinear relationship. We then used Ward’s minimum variance method to calculate the dissimilarity distance ddissimilarity and to perform hierarchical clustering. The dissimilarity distance thresholds ddis,thresh were incrementally selected with values ranging from 0.000 to 0.100, using a step size of 0.025.

It is highly possible that more than one feature exists for a given cluster, and we need to keep a single feature from each cluster. To overcome this, we used logistic regression with an Elastic Net penalty to provide the importance of each feature. As such, the feature with the highest magnitude Elastic Net coefficient for each cluster was selected. Feature selection was performed on the stratified k-fold (k=5) cross-validation dataset for each OAR separately. Similar to the approach with hyperparameter tuning, the final selection of features was decided by whichever set yielded the highest average AUC in the cross-validation datasets. Feature selection was also built in Python using the Scikit-learn module.

Bootstrapping is a repeated resampling method that can estimate the uncertainty of machine learning models. Models were fitted by repeatedly sampling data with replacement and evaluated on the out-of-bag samples. Here, 100 bootstrap samples were drawn for estimation and the standard deviation in the AUC (σ) from the 100 bootstrap samples was evaluated. The Z-test with bootstrapped standard deviation was used to determine any statistically significant difference in model performance using R software version 4.2.1.
Single-metric approach

A single geometric agreement metric can also be used as rudimentary binary classifier. Given the threshold, a single-metric classifier will consider the test OAR as unacceptable if the corresponding metric is higher or lower than the threshold (depending on the type of metric), and vice versa. In this study, 27 geometric agreement metric classifiers were established and evaluated using both the training and testing datasets. Only the top 5 metrics with the highest AUC were exhibited for each OAR. The ROC curve was used to evaluate the metrics’ discriminate ability.
Model validation

The final well-trained ML-MF model was used to evaluate the clinical acceptability of contours in the testing dataset and predictions were compared against the previously established clinical acceptability. The performance of the ML-MF model was evaluated quantitatively using precision, recall, and accuracy, and the time required from analyzing each case was recorded. In addition, the performance of the ML-MF model was compared against predictions made with Rhee’s and Men’s approaches. Following Rhee’s description, a threshold DSC value was determined such that it catches >70% of cases with errors (recall=0.7) in the cross-validation dataset. This threshold DSC value was then applied to the testing dataset to flag cases. It should be noted that due to the limited data sampling, the recall achieved in the testing dataset can deviate from 0.7. Further, for a better performance comparison with our ML-MF model, a second threshold DSC value was determined such that the recall achieved exactly matches that of ML-MF model in the testing dataset. These two approaches were named as “Rhee_orig” and “Rhee_recallmatch,” respectively. Following Men’s approach, threshold values for DSC and HD95 metrics were determined based on the means and standard deviations of these metrics in a benchmark dataset:
A contour was considered clinically acceptable if it passed either of these criteria.

McNemar’s test is a paired nonparametric statistical test, and it has been widely used to compare binary classifiers. In this study, the performance of the ML-MF model, Men’s approach, Rhee_recallmatch, and Rhee_orig were compared using McNemar’s test for unacceptable contours, acceptable contours, and were then combined.
External validation on model performance

To evaluate the generalizability of our model, 60 clinical HN cases from our institution were retrospectively analyzed. Since the training data originated from different institutions, the data from our institution are considered as “external data” from a ML perspective. The external dataset comprises 60 Brainstem contours, 55 Parotid_L contours, 58 Parotid_R contours, and 60 Mandible contours. Our model was then applied to these data to flag possible errors. If a contouring error was flagged, a radiation oncologist would then review the flagged contour without the aid of the DLAS contour. The radiation oncologist would either accept the model’s prediction as a true positive (TP) or reject model’s prediction as a false positive (FP). Later, the radiation oncologist was given an opportunity to adjust their reading by introducing the DLAS contour, and both reading results were recorded. Men’s approach and Rhee_orig were also applied to these data.
Evaluation tools of classification models

Receiver operating characteristic curves can be used as evaluation tools to understand the discriminative ability of classifiers, which summarizes the true positive rate (x-axis) and false positive rate (y-axis) using different thresholds. With different thresholds, the classifier would demonstrate different TP and FP rates. The trade-off should be made between the TP and FP to determine the appropriate threshold (cut-off point). The area under the ROC curve, AUC, is a commonly used metric to reflect the discriminative ability of classifiers across all possible thresholds. An AUC value of 0.5 means the classifier has no discriminative ability, while the higher the AUC value, the better the discriminative ability. If the AUC value is smaller than 0.5, it also means that the classifier has the potential to predict the positive class as the negative class. The ROC curve is not appropriate for classifiers with pre-defined thresholds, such as Men’s approach, Rhee_recallmatch, and Rhee_orig. Therefore, this study used confusion metrics and their derivative performance metrics (i.e., precision, recall, and accuracy) for the comparison involving classifiers with pre-defined thresholds.
RESULTS
Model performance in the cross-validation dataset

The results of the hierarchical cluster analysis for feature selection of the 27 geometric agreement metrics are shown in Figure 2. As the dissimilarity distance threshold value is varied, different numbers of feature clusters were selected. Within each descendent cluster, the feature with the highest elastic net coefficient was selected. This is illustrated in Figure 2, where Spearman threshold values of 0.025, 0.050, 0.050, and 0.100 were applied to Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible contours, respectively.

Table2 summarizes the number of features selected for a range of thresholds and the corresponding model performance in the cross-validation dataset. In addition, a model was also trained using only two, the most frequently used, contour evaluation metrics (DSC and HD values) as a comparison. For Parotid_L, model performance was significantly better (P<0.05, two-tailed Z test) when using multiple features compared against using only two features (DSC and HD). Features were selected based on which subset yielded the highest mean AUC in the cross-validation dataset. Analysis of the results found that the highest mean AUC was achieved using models trained with 17, 13, 12, and 11 features for the Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible contours, respectively. The ROC curves for the ML models with the highest averaged AUC are shown in Figure 3. The μ ± σ of the AUC achieved by the ML models are 0.902 ± 0.033, 0.888 ± 0.041, 0.908 ± 0.030, and 0.980±0.014 for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Patorid_R, and Mandible contours, respectively. For comparison, the highest AUC achieved from the single metric model is 0.876, 0.860, 0.874, and 0.974 using HD99, recall, DSC, and HD100 for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Patorid_R, and Mandible contours, respectively.
Model performance in the testing dataset

Upon successful feature selection, the ML-MF model was re-trained using the full training dataset. The fully trained model was then validated using the testing dataset. Figure 4 presents the ROC curves for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible contours using our model as well as single-metric models for comparison. As was observed in the cross-validation dataset, our model achieved a higher AUC compared to using any of the single-metric models.

Table 3 summarizes the discriminative capability for identifying OAR segmentation errors using our model, Rhee’s approach, and Men’s approach. Our ML-MF model achieved recall (precision) values of 0.842 (0.889), 0.762 (0.762), 0.727 (0.842), 0.773 (0.773) for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible contours, respectively. In the “Rhee_orig” approach, the threshold DSCRhee_orig values were evaluated as 0.779, 0.777, 0.778, and 0.860 and the recall (precision) achieved were 0.526 (0.909), 0.619 (0.765), 0.682 (0.882), 0.727 (0.586) for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible contours, respectively. In order to match the recall achieved by our model, The threshold DSCRhee_recallmatch was evaluated as 0.826, 0.800, 0.795, and 0.865 and the resulting recall (precision) achieved were 0.842 (0.571), 0.762 (0.640), 0.727 (0.762), and 0.818 (0.600) for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible contours, respectively.

In the Men’s approach, the thresholds DSCMen and HD95, Men were derived as 0.828 & 0.520 cm, 0.822 & 0.637 cm, 0.810 & 0.566 cm, and 0.876 & 0.385 cm for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible contours, respectively. Those thresholds were derived from the benchmark performance in Table 1. Using Men’s approach, a recall (precision) values of 0.737 (0.778), 0.524 (0.733), 0.772 (0.772), and 0773 (0.586) were achieved for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible respectively. Our ML-MF model carries out the highest accuracy among all approaches for all organs. The performance of different classifiers for (a) unacceptable, (b) acceptable, and (c) all including acceptable and unacceptable were evaluated and the p-values (McNemar’s test) were indicated in Table 4. The proposed ML-MF model performs significantly better than Rhee_orig in the brainstem unacceptable group and mandible acceptable group, and better than Rhee_recall in the brainstem acceptable and combined group as well as mandible acceptable group. From this, we conclude that our model achieves similar or better performance among existing approaches in the testing dataset.

To illustrate the error flagging capability of our model, Figure 5 shows different contouring errors that were successfully caught by our model (panels A-D). While our model is able to catch most of the errors, there are also a few cases that escaped the detection, one of which is shown in panel (E). For those escaped cases, the contouring errors had a large deviation on a small section and reasonable agreement for the rest of the volume, such as (E3). The features used in the ML-MF model do not change rapidly with small-area deviations, which may primarily contribute to the model missing this error.
Model generalizability in an external dataset

To test the generalizability, we applied our ML-MF model to 60 external HN cases. Of the 60 cases, 24 Brainstem, 15 Parotid_L, 17 Parotid_R, and 17 Mandible contours were flagged as potentially unacceptable. As shown in Table 5, 58.3%, 93.3%, 94.1%, and 58.8% of these flagged cases were confirmed by a radiation oncologist during their initial review. Additionally, when the DLAS contour was displayed for reference, the percentage of confirmed cases increased. It was observed by human inspection that a fair amount of brainstem contours in this external dataset have a few slice differences in the caudal direction, slightly failing the criteria. On the contrary, the TCIA dataset contains some unacceptable brainstem contours with more significant deviations in the caudal and radial direction. Therefore, there are less “easy” cases compared with the testing dataset from TCIA, which may account for the discrepancies in discriminative performance between the external dataset and the testing dataset. The existence of bite block (n=2) and dental artifact (n=1) on the flagged cases, as panel (E4-E5) in Figure 5 indicated, lowers the performance of ML-MF model due to inaccurate DLAS mandible contours. The confirm percentage lifts to 71.4% (10/14) if excluding edge cases.

Men’s approach and Rhee_orig where thresholds were developed from either benchmark dataset or TCIA training dataset were also applied to these external data for a comparison. Men’s approach flagged 32, 13, 20, and 22 suspectable cases, which included 16, 1, 5, and 11 false alarms as well as missed 1, 2, 1, and 1 errors for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible respectively. It should be noted that one of the Brainstem errors and one of the Mandible errors reported by Men’s approach were missed by ML-MF model. Rhee_orig flagged 10, 12, 14, and 51 cases, 6, 10, 13, and 10 are real errors, while missed 10, 3, 3, and 1 errors for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible respectively. Although Rhee’s method also flagged one extra case for Parotid_L contour that ML-MF model didn’t flag, it was rejected as a false-positive after careful review. For Mandible, Rhee_orig flagged more cases than TCIA dataset. One of the possible reasons is the frequent utilization of bite blocks, which drop down the performance of DLAS contours.
Computation time

For each patient case, DLAS contour generation took approximately 1 minute using an NVIDIA TITAN XP GPU. The calculation of geometric agreement metrics took approximately 20 seconds, and model training took approximately 90 seconds using an Intel(R) Xeon(R) E5–2630 v4 2.20GHz CPU. The time required for our model to flag cases was less than two seconds.
Discussion

We have demonstrated that the inclusion of multiple geometric agreement metrics in comparisons between manually-segmented and DLAS contours improves contouring error detection. The AUC achieved by using our model outperforms the AUC using existing approaches that rely only on DSC values (Rhee’s approach), or other single metrics such as HD or SDSC values. While the approach by Men et al uses both DSC and HD values, we have shown, the AUC achieved of Parotid_L ML-MF model using just these two metrics is still statistically inferior to that obtained with feature selection. In addition, this study shows that the inclusion of as many metrics as possible is not indicative of model prediction success. We see in Table 2, that the AUC achieved with a model using all 27 metrics is inferior to other models trained using fewer metrics. In this case, many of the metrics used are the same type with slightly modified parameters and therefore are highly correlated with each other. These highly correlated features can be detrimental to the learning process and prevent the model from capturing relevant information. Feature selection was a vital step that slightly improved model performance using less than half of the metrics while removing redundant features.

A table summarizing the selected features corresponding to different ddis,thresh values for each anatomy is presented in the supplementary materials. Each anatomy shows slightly different preferences for geometric features. The DSC, precision, recall, and HD100 are universal features in the ML-MF model for each anatomy. As the hierarchical dendrogram of different thresholds in the supplementary materials shows, one of the main reasons to explain this universalness is that these metrics are highly un-correlated with other metrics. Overlap (e.g. DSC, recall), boundary distance (e.g. HDx, MSD), and surface agreement (e.g. SDSCτ) metrics are all selected among different thresholds for all anatomies. This may indicate that the weakness from different types of metrics will be compensated by others. Therefore, we suggest that different classes of metrics should be involved in future studies.

The number of features needed for optimal classification is still unclear. In our study, we chose models with the highest mean ROC curve in the cross-validation dataset as final models; however, no powerful statistical evidence indicates they are statistically better than other models with different features. Many factors determine the feature selection process, such as data distribution, type of errors in unacceptable contours, and strategy used in feature selection. Feature selection is NP-hard challenge, and the complexity increases exponentially. Proposed feature selection finds locally rather than globally optimal solutions. However, it is clear that combining multiple metrics is superior to using simply DSC and HD values only.

The proposed ML-MF model was trained using TCIA images and was also tested using external data from our institution. The fractions of successfully flagged cases that were ultimately confirmed by a radiation oncologist, were 66.7%, 93.3%, 94.1%, and 58.8% for Brainstem, Parotid_L, Parotid_R, and Mandible contours respectively, which differ from the precision achieved in the TCIA testing dataset (88.9%, 76.2%, 84.2%, and 77.3% respectively). We believe that a primary source of this discrepancy is differing contouring practices for the images comprising each dataset. We have inspected contours from each dataset and have observed that a fair amount of TCIA cases only contoured parts of the brainstem that are within the treatment field. In this scenario, the DSC, HD95, and many metrics change dramatically, and it is obvious for a human to spot. Therefore, both our model and human inspection are highly successful in flagging these cases. In our institution, the entire brainstem is always contoured regardless of the treatment field and target position. The unacceptable contours are subtle to detect as they are not associated with large deviations. The shift in the distribution of types of error leads to a lower precision in our external dataset. Similarly, the parotids are generally contoured by different medical residents under training. It is likely the lack of experience magnifies errors and inter-observer variations; therefore, there could be a few more cases that has larger deviations in parotid contouring in our institution’s data, leading to higher reported precision values. The use of bite block in our institution also contributes to the discrepancy of mandible. The DLAS model used in this study unavoidably suffers from the lack of generalizability in the unseen data (i.e. bite blocks., such as panel (E5) in Figure 5). If we exclude the cases with either bite blocks or dental artifacts, the fraction of successfully flagged mandible cases would promote to 71.4% which closes to TCIA percentage.

Different metrics achieved the highest AUC for various anatomical sites in the single-metric approach. The different types of errors and anatomical sites may be the source of these differences. For instance, the brainstem is tube-shaped anatomy, and overlap metrics (e.g., DSC) might be more sensitive if the structure is under/over-contoured uniformly. In contrast, distance metrics (e.g., HD or MSD) are easier to catch errors if the structure is over/under-contoured in a specific direction. Through observation, the errors observed for brainstem contours frequently happen in the caudal (inferior) direction in the TCIA dataset, which leads to the highest AUC obtained using the HD99 in both the cross-validation and testing datasets. The common errors observed in the Mandible contours are (1) including teeth as part of mandible, (2) miss contouring coronoid process, as panel (D1-D2) in Figure 5 indicates. The HD100 can be utilized to catch those errors. Similarly, distance metrics are more insensitive than others for parotids due to their natures of irregularity and low contrast. The classification ability of a single metric is fragile and non-robust. For the Parotid_R contours, the DSC showed an AUC value of 0.874 in the cross-validation dataset, while the value dropped down to 0.782 in the testing dataset, as shown in Fig. 3 and Fig. 4. This may be due to the heterogeneous data distribution of error types between cross-validation and testing datasets. On the other hand, it implies the necessity of utilizing multiple geometric metrics to flag potential errors.

Figure 6 plots all contours studied based on their DSC and HD95 metric. The unacceptable contours were labelled in red and acceptable contours labelled in blue. As shown in the figure, the contours acceptability cannot be reliably differentiated with only DSC and HD95.

The shortcoming of the classifier solely relied on DSC can be reflected in the classifier performance of Rhee_orig in the Mandible external dataset. The dropped DLAS performance of mandible directly brings on that Rhee_orig flagged 85% (51 of 60) cases as suspectable. By considering more metrics, our ML-MF models were able to achieve better performance than other approaches that relies on only one or two metrics.

In this study, we considered the clinical acceptability of contours based on a single radiation oncologist’s interpretation of one set of contour guidelines. It is likely that a different radiation oncologist may score the cases differently, which can affect model training. The acknowledged inter-observer variation inevitably induces biases in all approaches based on human labeling. This fact highlights the weakness of our approach, in that the ML-MF model sacrifices the ability to generalize, but it is capable of learning individual radiation oncologists’ preferences. Future studies will be directed toward comparing different radiation oncologists’ judgments on the same set of cases and how this affects model performance.

The prediction thresholds were derived from cross-validation ROC curves using the nearest point to (0,1); however, thresholds can be flexibly defined considering the cost and clinical usage. The intended usage of QA models is to detect possible errors. Choosing a different threshold with higher error-catching capability, but more “false alarms,” is achievable. For classifiers with pre-defined thresholds, it is challenging to select different thresholds based on the clinical condition, even if some may achieve similar classification performance as the ML-MF model. The single-metric approach also provides the choice of thresholds; however, the robustness is doubtful, as discussed above. Additionally, the ML-ML model could catch more errors than the single-metric approach. The AUC achieved by the proposed model is higher than single-metric models in both the cross-validation and testing datasets for all organs except the Parotid_L in the testing dataset, where the approaches achieved the same AUC.

In this study, the brainstem, parotids, and mandible structures in the HN region were used to demonstrate the efficacy of our model. Aside from patient side effects related to brainstem parotid, and mandible structures, these were also chosen because there are sufficient clinically unacceptable contours for each structure in the TCIA public dataset. We have observed that 35% of the brainstem, and 40% of the parotids contours, and 43% of mandible contain deviations that exceed our tolerance. Other structures, such as eyes and brain, did not contain such high number of unacceptable contours. Since model training requires that the dataset contains sufficient examples of acceptable and unacceptable contours, we did not select these organs in this study. Furthermore, the acceptability of some structures, such as chiasm, and optical nerves, is highly subjective due to the lack of clear definitions on CT. These organs are generally recommended to be delineated on MRI. However, we expect that the proposed methodology will be applicable to other structures and other anatomic sites if there are sufficient examples of unacceptable contours.

Considering that all cases in both datasets were treated clinically, and that the contours had been reviewed and approved by attending radiation oncologists, the observed percentage of unacceptable contours raises concern. However, further review revealed that some of the deviations do not have significant clinical impact. Some cases in the TCIA HN-PET-CT dataset only contour structures in the treatment field. In these cases, even though the structure was under-contoured, it did not impact the evaluation of the maximum dose to the structure. Similarly, many of the over-contouring cases observed in our institution’s dataset were either far away from the target, and therefore had minimal dosimetric impact or simply provide a harmless over-protection of the structures. Meanwhile, some of the deviations may arise from either different contouring guidelines applied or the different interpretations under the same guideline. The similar phenomenon was observed on swallowing OARs by Brouwer et.al. Regardless, the observed percentage of missed contour errors shows that there is room for improvement in the current contouring practice. The inclusion of a contour QA tool can help dosimetrists or medical residents who create the initial contours to catch most errors prior to attending radiation oncologists’ review.
Conclusion

In this study, we developed a ML-based approach to achieve a more accurate flagging of manual contour errors by utilizing DLAS contours as a reference. This model determines the clinical acceptability of contours by combining multiple geometric agreement metrics between the DLAS and manual contours. The proposed QA method can easily be implemented in clinic practice to flag cases for further review and can help to reduce the total manual review time and labor, enhance the detectability of potential contour errors, and subsequently improve the safety and effectiveness of radiotherapy.
